newsitem.title: UK: Welsh oil spill harmed thousands of Britons -study.
newsitem.headline: Welsh oil spill harmed thousands of Britons -study.

text.p: An oil spill from a tanker that ran aground off the coast of Wales in February gave at least 5,000 Britons health problems ranging from nausea to depression, a local health authority study revealed on Tuesday.
More than 72,000 tonnes of oil was spilled when the Sea Empress ran on to rocks off Milford Haven, south Wales, on February 15. Around 200 kilometres (125 miles) of coastline was contaminated.

One in six people in the area suffered from headaches, nausea and sore throats after the spill and some suffered anxiety and depression after being caught up in the disaster, the study, published by Dyfed-Powys Health Authority, found.
People living within half a mile (one km) of oil-covered beaches had a higher incidence of physical and psychological illness than the rest of the population.
The authority estimated at least 5,000 people were likely to have suffered health problems in some way in February and March.

"There was a higher than normal incidence of headaches, nausea, runny nose, sore throat, cough and shortness of breath. Some people reported itchy skin, rashes and weakness. These are typical signs of exposure to oil," Ronan Lyons of the West Wales centre for Public Health said.

At least 2,000 birds were killed by oil from the Liberian-registered tanker and two nature reserves were affected, including one on Lundy Island, some 50 miles (80 km) south of the incident, famed for its colony of puffins.
The fishing and tourist industries in the area were disrupted for months.

The spillage was reckoned to be the worst to hit the British coastline since the 1967 wreck of the Torrey Canyon, which spilled 100,000 tonnes of crude oil on to the coast of Cornwall in southwest England.

A follow-up study looking at the longer-term effects of the Sea Empress spillage may be undertaken in a year or so. The Department of Transport is still conducting an official inquiry into the disaster.
